entities.summary:
Rodrigo Sánchez de Arévalo (1404, Santa María la Real de Nieva – 1470-10-13, Rome) was a prominent Spanish churchman, diplomat, historian, and political theorist whose intellectual contributions significantly shaped Castilian political thought and papal authority during the tumultuous 15th century. Serving successive Castilian monarchs, Juan II and Enrique IV, and later popes Pius II and Paul II, Sánchez de Arévalo navigated the complex interplay of secular and ecclesiastical power, becoming a staunch defender of both royal prerogative and papal supremacy against the rising tide of conciliarism. His writings, particularly *Summa de re publica* and *Defensor fidei*, established him as a leading intellectual voice of his era in Southern Europe.

His career began in Castile, where he earned doctorates in canon and civil law and served as a royal ambassador for Juan II, participating in critical diplomatic missions, including negotiations with Aragon. Under Enrique IV, he continued his service, eventually being appointed Bishop of Oviedo (1456), then Zamora (1465), and finally Calahorra (1467). However, his most influential period unfolded in Rome, where he served as a curial official for Pope Pius II, acting as a pivotal figure in papal diplomacy and intellectual defense. During this time, he composed his most significant works, which synthesized classical, patristic, and scholastic thought to articulate a robust vision of political and ecclesiastical order.
